TX.why: Governor-elect Hinojosa backs an immediate moratorium with no firm end date: until the session ends (May 31, 2027) or terms are met (no subsidies, proof household bills won't rise). Abbott's permit/ERCOT freeze is already in place. Modo: ~10 GW of expected build stopped, 24 GW under construction uncertain, Batch Zero likely slips to summer 2027. Jefferies: ~13 GW of announced projects at risk.

GA.why: Governor-elect Lance Bottoms backs an immediate statewide pause on large data centers; PSC races also turned on Georgia Power's data center expansion.

OH.why: Governor-elect Acton backs a conditional moratorium: new campuses paused unless they pay 100% of their utility costs, use union labour and meet state environmental rules (Modo counts this as new terms, not a stop). Kept at tier 5 because 14+ municipalities passed bans or limits on Nov 3 and the state already halted tax credits for new projects.

MI.why: Governor-elect Benson backs a conditional statewide moratorium (cost, labour and environmental terms); local opposition at Saline Twp (Stargate) and a recall in Mason.

PA.why: State Sen. Muth's three-year hyperscale moratorium bill and ratepayer act; PJM cost-allocation fights.

VA.why: No ban, but tax-break review and Dominion grid queue; Loudoun limits.

IL.why: Pritzker stopped signing new data center incentive agreements; local ballot restrictions and Bloomington moratorium advisory. Exposed capacity sits mostly in ComEd territory (PJM).

KS.why: Holscher (D) leads by ~7,600 votes after the mail deadline and has been called the winner by several outlets (audit pending, no concession); she would block approvals until guardrails exist. Emporia already banned high-impact data centers after a 1 GW proposal.

ME.why: Governor-elect Pingree backs an immediate statewide moratorium; eight towns had already passed temporary moratoriums.

NH.why: Governor Ayotte, re-elected, plans to propose a statewide moratorium (opposed the Bow plan); local 12-month permit moratoriums.

NV.why: Democrats gained the governorship; water limits.

WI.why: Governor-elect Crowley backs a conditional moratorium on new construction (similar terms to Ohio and Michigan); local zoning fights. Modo groups Wisconsin's pause with the time-limited delays.

IN.why: State friendly, but local bans and Lebanon pushback.

MN.why: Moratorium bills introduced; water and clean-energy rules.

AZ.why: Water is the binding limit; Phoenix-area restrictions.

LA.why: State actively courts projects (Act 730 rebates); prediction markets price ~18.5% chance of a moratorium by end-2027.

OK.why: State friendly; one mayor recalled in Yukon over a hyperscale deal.

NM.why: Governor-elect Haaland vowed an immediate moratorium by executive order. Project Jupiter is under construction, but its on-site power air permit (Dec 7 hearing) is the kind of non-construction permit a pause can hold up.

NC.why: Duke rate cases; mixed local reception.

SC.why: Congressional flips on data center records; Santee Cooper capacity.

KY.why: Burgin mayor who approved a hyperscale project lost to a write-in.

OR.why: Governor Kotek is holding state land and environmental permits for new data centers until July 2027; water and clean-energy constraints.

WA.why: Hydro capacity tight; tax break debates.

NJ.why: New rate class for data centers advancing.

NY.why: Executive Order 62 pauses state environmental permits for projects of 50 MW or more (time-limited); grid and climate-law constraints.

MS.why: Courts hyperscalers (Amazon $10B, xAI power plant); little organised opposition.

AL.why: Pro-development; TVA and Alabama Power capacity.

AR.why: Friendly regime; Entergy Arkansas and SWEPCO.

ND.why: Harwood voters rejected extra review 3-to-1; abundant land and power.

WY.why: Gas and wind, pro-development; Google's $17B Cheyenne campus (ex-Crusoe/Tallgrass site) pays for all its own power. Watch: a University of Wyoming poll shows only ~30% support and Congressman-elect Chuck Gray opposes new AI data centers.

WV.why: Power Generation and Data Center Act lets projects build their own power.

capexPerGW.why: All-in AI campus cost incl. GPUs/racks (~$30–35B) and shell, power and cooling (~$10–12B)

equipShare.why: Share of capex that is taxable IT equipment

salesTax.why: Texas state 6.25% + local up to 2%; similar exemptions in GA/OH

selfPower.why: Paying for grid upgrades or behind-the-meter gas (~$2,000/kW for half the load)

community.why: Water recycling, community benefit agreements, union labour premium

sunk.why: Site-specific spend written off on relocation: land, interconnection deposits, design, long-lead electrical gear re-routing

revPerGW.why: GPU cloud revenue per GW-year at current rental rates

pauseDelay.why: Texas: GLJ sees 12–18 months for projects with power but no state permit; Modo sees 6–9 months if the pause lifts when the session ends (May 2027), but warns short pauses tend to run long

msft.view: Least exposed hyperscaler: Fairwater Wisconsin and Atlanta are built (Wisconsin's second phase now sits under Crowley's conditional pause, and Georgia's new phases under Bottoms'), and the only big at-risk Texas item is the 900 MW Abilene campus that is not yet energised. Microsoft is now pulling back from rented capacity (Oracle deal wound down, Nscale Texas option declined, tighter oversight of IREN and Nebius) and favouring its own builds, which shifts delivery risk onto its suppliers. The catch is that third-party delays already cut September-quarter capex by about $5B, so own-build slippage now shows up directly in Azure capacity.
moves: Shift Abilene phase to Wyoming/Iowa
Consolidate to a few neocloud partners and own builds
Fund grid upgrades to keep Atlanta expansions moving

amzn.view: Exposure is now larger than it looked: two 1 GW+ Ohio campuses (Jeffersonville, Beech Road) are under construction in a tier-5 state, on top of Georgia's Butts and Covington builds. Trenton's ban hits only the 600-acre township expansion, not the four buildings already rising in the city. AWS has the deepest bench of friendly-state sites (Mississippi, Indiana, Pennsylvania nuclear, ~2 GW in central Virginia), so the cost is timing, not lost demand.
moves: Redirect Ohio phases to Indiana/Mississippi
Accelerate Susquehanna nuclear campus
Offer ratepayer-protection tariffs in Georgia

googl.view: Texas is the problem: Armstrong (~1.07 GW), Wilbarger (~0.85 GW) and Meitner in Gray County (~0.84 GW) are under construction and Haskell is planned, all under Hinojosa's pause. Google is already showing the workaround: two days after the election it took over Crusoe's Wyoming site for $17B and pledged to pay for 100% of the power, mostly from on-site fuel cells. That template (own power, no ratepayer cost, air cooling) is the one most likely to win approvals under the new regimes, but it raises cost per GW, and losing Texas's sales-tax exemption alone is material at this scale. The stock's weakness is mostly sector sentiment; its site risk is real but the most manageable among the big builders.
moves: Move Texas phases to Wyoming, Oklahoma (Mayes) and Arkansas
Self-supply power (Bloom/AEP, Intersect) to sidestep grid-cost fights
Phase Texas builds to fit grandfathered permits

meta.view: Most exposed hyperscaler: El Paso (1 GW JV) in Texas, Piqua (1.4 GW) blocked in Ohio, and the 5 GW Hyperion bet in Louisiana. Two new pressure points landed Monday: a Texas bill package targets the El Paso abatement and the sales-tax exemption, and a Louisiana lawsuit challenges the fast-track the utility needs on Dec 10 to approve Hyperion's seven gas plants, so even the friendly state now carries legal timing risk. Meta pays for that power itself, which is its best defence, and its president says at least one newly elected governor wants to meet after inauguration. Negative quarterly free cash flow makes delay costs bite harder than at peers; the stock's weakness reflects real site risk, not just sentiment.
moves: Concentrate on Hyperion and Lebanon, Indiana
Lock in the Dec 10 Louisiana approval before the lawsuit is heard
Lease surplus compute and build overseas (management flagged)

orcl.view: Three Stargate sites in Texas (Abilene, Shackelford 2 GW) and every hedge site is now in a pause state: Michigan (Benson, conditional), Wisconsin's Lighthouse (Crowley, conditional) and New Mexico's Jupiter (Haaland, immediate moratorium). Most are under construction and should be grandfathered from new approvals, but state permits, on-site power permits and ERCOT large-load service are still exposed. Oracle already sent a force majeure notice at Jupiter, lenders are testing its debt, and Microsoft is winding down its older rented capacity. Debt-funded with negative free cash flow, Oracle is the hyperscaler where financing and permits compound. Oracle is guiding to ~10 GW of AI data center capacity by May 2028, so most of that target runs through these pause states.
moves: Rush Shackelford buildings to energise before Jan 19
Secure Jupiter's air permit (Dec 7 hearing)
Re-sell freed Microsoft capacity to OpenAI

sbank.view: Milam County (1.2 GW, Texas) and Lordstown (Ohio, town ban) are both in hostile states. SoftBank/SB Energy owns the power at Milam, which helps, but OpenAI's funding chain is leveraged and sensitive to delay.
moves: Use SB Energy generation to avoid grid-cost fights
Re-site Lordstown capacity

spcx.view: Live today: ~1.7 GW in Memphis (SpaceX's Sep 30 nameplate). The near-term build (Colossus 2 Building 3, ~0.8 GW) is in Tennessee/Mississippi, where neither governor backs a pause. The exposure is the 2027 plan: Musk targets at least 13 GW by end-2027, and the ~10.5 GW not yet sited is reportedly headed to new Texas sites, which now fall under Hinojosa's pause. Risk raised from Low-Medium to Medium on that basis.
moves: Keep near-term growth in Memphis/Southaven
Site 2027 builds outside Texas or energise before new rules
Behind-the-meter gas and batteries to avoid grid fights

crwv.view: CoreWeave's own sites are mostly outside Texas, but it is the tenant at Texas developer sites (Galaxy Helios, Core Scientific Denton) and runs six Texas locations. Its letter asked Hinojosa to let permitted projects finish, but she has now said she will use the permits that even started projects still need, so contracted Texas capacity is not fully safe. Monday's 5.6% bounce on a Wayve training deal is sentiment; credit is the real signal, with five-year CDS above 1,240 bp and 2031 bonds yielding over 16%. Tuesday's results need to show the backlog converting and funding for 2027 lined up; Microsoft trimming its neocloud roster is the other overhang.
moves: Lock in grandfathering for permitted Texas builds with the transition team
Lean on North Dakota (Applied Digital) and Pennsylvania
Prioritise energised capacity in contracts

nbis.view: Live US footprint is small (Kansas City, Vineland), but the pipeline is now large: Independence, Missouri (1.2 GW, approved), Highridge in Pennsylvania (1.2 GW, a tier-4 state) and Birmingham, Alabama (~0.3 GW, where the city is weighing a moratorium). Its 5 GW contracted-power target for end-2026 is company-wide, so ~1.9 GW is not tied to a disclosed site and likely includes Europe. Near-zero net debt and prepayments mean Nebius can wait out delays better than most neoclouds.
moves: Lead with Missouri (approved) while Pennsylvania clears
Keep Finland/Israel capacity as a hedge

iren.view: Childress (750 MW, energised) and the 2 GW Sweetwater site are both in Texas. The Childress slip to January–February is a customer-requested network redesign, not a regulatory block, and backlog rose to $20.3B, so the 20% rebound on Nov 6 was earned. Sweetwater's energisation is still ERCOT-gated and Microsoft is now auditing its suppliers, so concentration on one customer and one state keeps this High.
moves: Deliver Horizons 2–4 inside Microsoft grace periods
Energise Sweetwater before new rules
Diversify beyond Microsoft (frontier-lab contract signed)

apld.view: North Dakota sites; Harwood voters backed the project 3-to-1, the one industry win on Nov 3. The 14% fall was sentiment; fundamentally a beneficiary as capacity migrates north.
moves: Market as the friendly-state alternative

glxy.view: Helios in Dickens County, Texas, is the whole AI story; further phases need ERCOT approvals.
moves: Phase within existing interconnection

cifr.view: All Texas: Barber Lake (Fluidstack, Google backstop), Black Pearl (300 MW for AWS, first phase live) and Stingray (100 MW for Amazon) are under the Texas pause, and Colchis (1 GW conditional ERCOT base load, 2028) is further out. Long AWS and Google-backed leases lower financing risk, but every site needs Texas permits and ERCOT service.
moves: Lean on AWS and Google-backed leases
Energise Black Pearl and Stingray before new rules

frmi.view: 11 GW Amarillo plan with no anchor tenant: the purest play on Texas approvals and the most likely to be delayed indefinitely.
moves: Seek federal (DOE) land or nuclear route

crusoe.view: Crusoe sold its Cheyenne, Wyoming site to Google on Nov 6 after failing to sign a customer there, so it loses a 1.8 GW development but recovers its pre-development spend. The bigger exposure is Texas: Crusoe built Stargate Abilene and Google's Goodnight campus, and its ~1 GW Project Hyper in Childress is under construction under the Texas pause. Crusoe now cites more than 6 GW contracted and 40 GW+ in its pipeline, but losing Wyoming to the end customer shows hyperscalers taking projects in-house.

qts.view: QTS built Microsoft's Fairwater Atlanta (previously double-counted here as a separate Fayetteville campus). Its own large AI footprint is Richmond, Virginia (~560 MW IT live), a mixed-risk state, so direct exposure is the Georgia pause hitting future Atlanta phases.
moves: Shift new Atlanta phases to Alabama/Mississippi
Keep expanding Richmond

dev.t: Hinojosa told the New York Times she cannot halt every permitted project but will use the remaining permits that even started data centers still need to hold them until protections pass, a wider reach than the 'new approvals only' reading of her pause.

On the first day of Texas bill pre-filing, State Rep. Vince Perez filed bills to repeal the state's data center sales-tax exemption, cap abatements at 10 years with a public vote on every new phase (aimed at Meta's El Paso deal), and bar shifting the El Paso gas plant's cost onto other customers.

Louisiana landowner and citizen groups sued the state utility commission over the 'Lightning Directive' fast track that Entergy plans to use on Dec 10 to approve seven gas plants and transmission for Meta's Hyperion; the same pathway is used for Applied Digital's Rapides Parish site.

The Senate held its first 60-vote test Monday evening on the permitting bill that makes 20 MW+ data centers pay their full grid costs; TD Cowen cut its odds of the bill passing to 25% from 40% after the election.

Constellation beat estimates and raised 2026 guidance, with about 8.5 GW of long-term power deals signed this year including Amazon and Google; power names rebounded (Constellation +10%, Bloom +14%, Vertiv +10%, GE Vernova +7%) as buyers are clearly still signing.

Nvidia fell 4.3% after its board opened an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang over an alleged Chinese intelligence contact, while AMD jumped 13% on an Oppenheimer upgrade and Google choosing EPYC CPUs to host its new TPU 8tx; the S&P 500 rose 2.3% and CoreWeave 5.6% (Wayve deal) before Tuesday's earnings.

CoreWeave's CEO wrote to Texas governor-elect Hinojosa asking that already-permitted projects be allowed to finish and offering to help write standards for new ones; the letter names its Austin, Denton, Dickens County, Plano, Richardson and Round Rock sites.

Kansas: Democrat Cindy Holscher's lead held at about 7,600 votes after the mail-ballot deadline and several outlets have called the race for her, though a close-race audit is still running and Masterson has not conceded.

Hinojosa asked Texas Parks and Wildlife to take no action during the transition on selling 1,300 acres of Boca Chica state park land next to SpaceX's Starbase, an early sign she will use agency appointees to slow Musk-linked projects.

Susquehanna: of ~148 GW of AI training capacity planned for 2025–2030, about 60 GW (40%) still awaits approvals and up to 12 GW (8%) could be cancelled in a worst case, almost all in 2028–2030; most 2027 projects are already permitted.
Reuters: Nvidia is financing billions of dollars of new CoWoS packaging capacity at ASE's SPIL unit, a sign the chip supply chain is still capacity-bound despite the US permitting scare.

Google bought Crusoe's Cheyenne, Wyoming site and will spend $17B building it itself, paying for all of its power from a 702 MW AEP fuel-cell plant built with Bloom cells; Crusoe exits after failing to land a customer.
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar said the company will keep building US capacity despite the midterm sweep, is raising fresh capital, and will stop using NDAs with public officials on new sites.

The Senate permitting bill's final text, up for a vote Monday, keeps the rule that new data centers of 20 MW or more pay the full cost of their grid service and lets states charge more or require own generation.

Neoclouds bounced Friday (IREN +16% on doubled AI revenue, CoreWeave +6.6%, Applied Digital +9%) but remain roughly half their October levels; Bernstein cut IREN's target to $55 and named IREN and Cipher the most Texas-exposed. CoreWeave reports Nov 10, Nebius Nov 12.
Bloomberg Intelligence expects the election to cut 2027 AI infrastructure spending by 5–7% of ~$1.4T and up to 10 GW of capacity to miss next year's online dates.

Added named campuses from filings: Nebius Independence (1.2 GW, approved), Pennsylvania Highridge (1.2 GW) and Birmingham; Applied Digital Delta Forge 1 (LA) and Polaris Forge 3 (ND); Cipher Black Pearl and Stingray (AWS) and Colchis. Company targets beyond named sites (SpaceX, Oracle, Nebius) now show as Planned, not yet sited.
SpaceX reported 1.7 GW of nameplate compute at Sep 30 (1.4 GW in June); on the Q3 call Musk targeted 2.5–3 GW by end-2026 and at least 13 GW by end-2027.

Campus figures moved to total facility power (Epoch AI, Cleanview) and re-verified; added AWS Ohio and central Virginia builds, Google's Wilbarger and Meitner campuses, Crusoe Childress, Nexus Hubbard and Nebius Independence.
Trenton's 25 MW+ ban passed with ~80% on Nov 3, but AWS's four-building in-city campus is unaffected; only the proposed 600-acre township expansion is blocked.

Data check against Epoch AI: Colossus 2 corrected to ~946 MW IT operating in Memphis (was shown as 1 GW under construction in Mississippi); campuses now show operating vs planned GW, Fairwater Atlanta/QTS double count removed, nine Epoch-tracked campuses added.
New Mexico's governor-elect Haaland has vowed an executive-order moratorium; Modo flags that on-site power permits like Project Jupiter's air permit could stall under-construction builds.

Modo Energy: 256 GW (40%) of tracked US data center capacity sits in states whose governors back pauses; at face value 11 GW of expected build stops (10 GW in Texas), and 2030 national capacity falls only ~3 GW once projects reallocate to MISO, SPP and the West.
Microsoft is winding down its 2023 deal to rent AI capacity from Oracle, saying the older Nvidia hardware no longer meets its needs.
Vistra raised 2026 guidance and set 2027 targets; it blamed softer ERCOT prices partly on the Texas data center permit pause, which it does not see as lasting.
IREN pushed its $4B+ run-rate target to January (possibly late February) after Microsoft asked for network changes at Childress; AI cloud revenue nearly tripled and the stock rose 20% the next day.
Bloomberg: Microsoft is tightening oversight of neocloud projects (Nebius, IREN, Nscale), walking away from sites it sees as risky and favouring its own data centers over new leases.
ING is auctioning about $500M of data center loans, including a slice of Project Jupiter debt in New Mexico, where Oracle has issued a force majeure notice and an air-permit hearing is set for Dec 7.
Hinojosa told CNN she is not ruling data centers out but wants a pause until laws protect Texans and give communities a say; markets read it as softer than feared.
Meta president says data center construction will be very challenging; every hyperscaler weighing building outside the US.
Jefferies trims US incremental capacity to 112.8 GW by 2030 from 122.4 GW; expects new starts to migrate to friendlier states.
UBS: ~30% of expected 2028 additions at risk, Texas alone 18 GW; data centers more likely to pay for grid upgrades.
Texas governor-elect Hinojosa promises to extend the data center moratorium until the Legislature passes protections; local communities would get a vote.
Ohio: at least 14 municipalities pass bans or limits; Trenton closes annexation route for ~1 GW Amazon campus, Piqua targets 1.4 GW Meta campus.
GLJ: Texas projects with power but no state permit face 12–18 month delays; projects lacking both could move to Louisiana and Oklahoma.

GW at each pause's face value, of the pipeline not yet operating

pts: Five winners back an immediate moratorium (TX, GA, NM, ME, NH); three back conditional ones (OH, MI, WI); NY, OR and IL already have governor pauses; KS is too close to call.
ERCOT has all 119 GW of its tracked capacity under a pause-backing governor; PJM has 60 GW (26%) exposed, mostly Ohio and ComEd Illinois.
A one-year ERCOT pause leaves Texas ~9 GW behind by 2035; two years or more ~13 GW. MISO, SPP and the West pick up most of it.
Most exposure is paper: of 242 GW not yet operating, 41 GW is under construction; in every pause state at least 61% is only announced or waiting on a grid connection.

spcx.basis: Company-wide nameplate compute. Year-end targets from Musk on the Q3 call; the ~11 GW 2027 jump has no named sites beyond Colossus 2 Building 3 and planned Texas sites. The 13 GW is Musk’s stated ambition, not committed sites.

orcl.now: 850 MW added in Q1 FY27 (quarterly addition, not fleet size)
orcl.basis: AI data center capacity, company-wide (investor day, Oct 28, 2026); ~7 GW of it is still to be added. CEO in Mar 2026: 10 GW+ secured, coming online over three years.

amzn.now: Added 3.9 GW in 2025 (addition, not total capacity)
amzn.basis: Jassy, Feb 2026: “double it again by the end of 2027.” AWS does not disclose its total GW; the Q3 2026 call gave capex only ($220B in 2026, “meaningfully more” in 2027).

msft.now: 24 new data centers added in the Sep quarter
msft.basis: Nadella, Oct 2025: roughly double the total datacenter footprint over two years. No GW figures given; calendar 2026 capex ~$170B.

meta.basis: No company GW total. Zuckerberg: “tens of GW” over this decade, with no year attached (Jan 2026). Hyperion raised to 5 GW in Jul 2026: first 2 GW by 2030, full 5 GW around 2032, pending Louisiana PSC approval of Entergy’s gas plants.

googl.basis: Alphabet gives capex, not GW. 2026 capex $195–205B was reaffirmed in Q3 (raised from $190B in Q2). For 2027 the CFO said only that capex will “increase significantly”; the >$300B figure circulating is a press estimate, not company guidance. The “double every six months” goal is AI serving capability (including software efficiency), not physical GW.

crwv.basis: Company-wide. This page tracks only CoreWeave’s three named owned/leased campuses (~0.95 GW); most active power sits in colocation sites not listed here, so the % at risk covers the tracked campuses only. Active power target set with Q2 2026 results (Aug 2026); Q3 results not yet out.

nbis.basis: Contracted = secured power, not live. Management expects 800 MW–1 GW connected by end-2026, active through H1 2027 (Q2 2026 call); deployment of more than 1 GW a year from 2027 (Q2 2026 letter).
